item.title: SeqKD Cuts Cost of Agentic Shopping Assistant While Preserving Quality
item.description:
SeqKD Cuts Cost of Agentic Shopping Assistant While Preserving Quality

You built a shopping assistant on a frontier model, and it works. When a shopper asks for “a black waist bag under twenty dollars from a shop with at least 4.5 stars,” the agent searches the catalog, inspects candidates, checks the constraints, and commits to a recommendation. The assistant is not a single model call; it runs a loop of search → read results → refine → verify → decide. Each loop may invoke the frontier model many times, and you pay for every call on every shopper. At production scale that per‑task cost compounds, erodes ROI, and can stop the project from shipping.

🔧 Why a Smaller Model?

  • A smaller model is faster to respond and cheaper to host.
  • The trade‑off is quality: a smaller model usually falls short on the task, which is why the larger one was chosen.

📚 Sequence‑Level Knowledge Distillation (SeqKD)

  • Goal: Transfer the behavior of the larger “teacher” model into a smaller “student” model.
  • Method: The teacher generates high‑quality responses; a student is trained on those responses with supervised fine‑tuning (SFT).
  • Input: Only the teacher’s text output – no access to logits, no reinforcement‑learning infrastructure, works even with a closed or API‑only teacher.
  • Benefit: Retains much of the teacher’s quality at the student’s speed and cost.

🛠 How SeqKD Works for an Agent

  1. Generate trajectories – For each input, the teacher produces a full reasoning trajectory: search queries, tool calls, observations, and final decision, each step conditioned on the previous ones.
  2. Collect dataset – The teacher’s text responses become a reusable dataset; you can train or test multiple students without regenerating data.
  3. Supervised fine‑tuning – Train the student on the whole trajectory so it learns the multi‑step reasoning, not just a single answer paragraph.
  4. Evaluation – A benchmark with a programmatic scorer can filter the teacher‑generated trajectories to keep only those that solve the task.

✅ Benefits of SeqKD

  • Cost‑effective – After the student is deployed you no longer pay frontier model prices for every request.
  • Portable – Works with any teacher that can return text, even if you cannot read its weights or logits.
  • High‑quality reasoning – Strong small reasoning models (e.g., DeepSeek‑R1 distilled models) have been built this way by fine‑tuning on teacher reasoning traces.
  • Reusable data – The generated answers persist as a dataset for future training or testing.

🚀 Practical Setup (AWS)

  • An AWS account with an IAM role for SageMaker AI that has read/write access to an S3 bucket and permission to invoke the teacher model.
  • A frontier teacher model to generate the trajectories (the walkthrough uses one on Amazon Bedrock).
  • Use an ml.m5.4xlarge instance at minimum for the notebook environment, since data preparation and local scoring run on its CPU.

📈 When to Use SeqKD

  • When an agentic application needs to run at scale and the per‑call cost of a frontier model is prohibitive.
  • When you lack access to the teacher’s logits or fine‑tuning APIs.
  • When you have a domain or task with no existing high‑quality labels, but you can generate them with the teacher.

SeqKD lets you keep the reasoning power of a large model while deploying a lean, inexpensive student that can handle the full multi‑step agentic workflow.

#AI #KnowledgeDistillation #AgenticAI #ECommerce

Source: Build efficient agents with knowledge distillation on Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation Improves Knowledge Transfer from Large Models
item.description:
Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation Improves Knowledge Transfer from Large Models

From Solver Trajectories to Teaching Trajectories: Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation was submitted on 27 Oct 2026 to the Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence category. The paper introduces a new approach to knowledge distillation from large reasoning models (LRMs).

🔍 Overview

  • Traditional distillation often uses raw teacher trajectories as supervision.
  • This creates a mismatch because advanced LRMs are optimized as strong solvers via reward‑driven post‑training (e.g., RLHF), not as teachers that produce reasoning processes smaller models can easily learn.
  • Smaller models have different “cognitive capacities” than their larger teachers, so directly imitating raw trajectories can be ineffective and typically needs many high‑quality samples.

🧩 How it works

  • The authors propose Cognition‑Aligned Reasoning Distillation (CARD), an RL‑based framework that transforms existing solver trajectories into teaching trajectories aligned with the student’s cognition.
  • CARD avoids expensive resampling by directly converting the original trajectories.
  • Optimization relies on two reward signals:
    1. Distribution Alignment Reward – matches the student’s predictive distribution.
    2. Logical Coherence Reward – reduces misleading failed reasoning steps.

⚙️ Key details

  • CARD is evaluated across multiple student models and settings.
  • Results show CARD outperforms distillation from raw teacher trajectories in in‑domain settings.
  • CARD also achieves substantial gains in out‑of‑distribution performance.

🚀 Availability

  • The code for CARD is released at the provided https URL.

💡 Why it matters

  • By aligning teacher trajectories with the student’s cognition, CARD addresses the mismatch between solver‑focused training of LRMs and the learning needs of smaller models, reducing the need for large numbers of high‑quality teacher samples.

#knowledge-distillation #large-models #reinforcement-learning

Source: From Solver Trajectories to Teaching Trajectories: Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation

item.title: Fisher Utility Weighting Boosts On-Policy Distillation Efficiency
item.description:
Fisher Utility Weighting Boosts On-Policy Distillation Efficiency

On‑policy distillation (OPD) is gaining traction as a cheaper alternative to reinforcement learning, but selecting which student‑generated tokens to supervise remains a challenge. A new study derives token importance directly from the distillation objective and introduces Fisher Utility Weighting (FUW), a continuous, mean‑normalized weighting scheme that consistently improves OPD performance.

🔍 Overview

  • Traditional token‑selection methods for OPD prioritize positions visited by the student using signals such as uncertainty, teacher‑student disagreement, and mismatch direction.
  • The authors instead ask: how much can each token’s loss decrease under an equal local KL budget on the student’s predictive distribution?
  • The answer is a utility score \(s_t = g_t^{\top} F_t^{\dagger} g_t\), where \(g_t\) is the logit gradient and \(F_t\) is the categorical Fisher matrix.

🧩 How It Works

  • Utility derivation: The utility measures the maximum loss reduction achievable with a local trust‑region (KL) constraint.
  • Objective‑specific forms
    • For reverse‑KL, the utility equals the student‑weighted variance of the student‑teacher log‑probability ratio.
    • For forward‑KL, it equals the Pearson \(\chi^2\) divergence.
  • The appropriate utility follows automatically from the chosen KL direction.

⚙️ Key Details

  • The utility is instantiated as Fisher Utility Weighting (FUW), a continuous token weight that is mean‑normalized across a sequence.
  • When evaluated on shared training checkpoints, several independently motivated criteria—student entropy, KL disagreement, and TIP—concentrate importance on nearly the same tokens at a 50 % selection fraction; they diverge at stricter fractions and for direction‑specific criteria.
  • Controlled token flips illustrate the practical impact of teacher corrections:
    • Single‑token flips give modest gains on failed trajectories.
    • Repeated flips raise accuracy from 28.4 % to 74.5 %, approaching the teacher’s 76.9 %.
    • Mass‑ and KL‑based selection outperform random flips by 15–18 percentage points at comparable counts.
  • Selective intervention remains useful after OPD, although higher argmax agreement does not consistently improve accuracy across model pairs.

📊 Results

Objective Improvement Range (macro points)
Reverse‑KL 1.35 – 4.0
Forward‑KL 1.08 – 2.71
  • These gains are measured across seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three Qwen‑3 student‑teacher pairs.
  • FUW matches or exceeds existing selective methods while relying on a single closed‑form score derived from the training objective.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Provides a principled, objective‑driven way to identify the most valuable teacher corrections, eliminating the need for handcrafted heuristics.
  • Improves OPD efficiency and final performance, making it a more viable alternative to full‑scale reinforcement learning for large language models.
  • Demonstrates that token‑level utility can be computed directly from the distillation loss, enabling better allocation of supervision budget during training.

#OnPolicyDistillation #FisherUtility #MachineLearning #KnowledgeDistillation

Source: Token Utility for On-Policy Distillation via Local Trust-Region Optimization Source: Demystifying On-Policy Distillation: Where Does the Teacher’s Advantage Live? Source: Beyond Corrected Actions: Training LLM Agents on Textual Critiques
